Monetary policy and portfolio positioning
The Federal Reserve (Fed) resumed its interest-rate cutting cycle on September 17, following 
a pause since December 2024. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) lowered the 
federal funds rate by 25 basis points (0.25%) to 4.00%–4.25% in September and another 
25 basis points (0.25%) to 3.75%–4.00% in October.1 In its statement, the FOMC noted 
that economic uncertainty remains elevated and that downside risks to employment 
have increased. The Fed also confirmed it will maintain the current pace of balance-sheet 
reductions, allowing $5 billion in U.S. Treasury securities and $35 billion in agency 
mortgage-backed securities to roll off each month.
The resumption of the Fed’s rate-cutting cycle came as little surprise to market participants. 
Recent data releases indicate that economic activity moderated during the first half of the 
year with the unemployment rate edging higher amid slowing job gains. Inflation remains 
somewhat elevated. Despite these headwinds, the FOMC raised its median gross domestic 
product (GDP) forecasts for 2025 and 2026 by 0.2% each, to 1.6% and 1.8%, respectively. It 
also lowered its unemployment projection by 0.1% for 2026 to 4.4%, while leaving its 2025 
estimate unchanged at 4.5%.2 Our outlook for year-end 2026 anticipates U.S. economic 
growth of 2.4%, a peak unemployment rate of 4.9%, and a continued gradual decline in 
inflation toward the Fed’s 2.0% target.
After back-to-back rate cuts in September and October, we expect an additional cut at 
December's meeting, with further easing in 2026. Over the next 15 months, monetary policy 
will likely be shaped by evolving economic data trends, shifting outlooks, and the balance of 
risks. Given this backdrop, we believe the Fed will remain flexible, adopting a measured, 
data-driven approach as it works to fulfill its dual mandate of price stability and full 
employment, rather than committing to a predetermined policy path. 
Our assessment of interest rates and U.S. Treasury yields 
Markets and investors will closely monitor this year’s one remaining Fed meeting — 
scheduled for December 10 — for signals of meaningful shifts in the broader macroeconomic 
outlook, including financial and geopolitical developments. In our view, the Fed is likely to 
implement additional rate cuts into early 2026 if signs of economic slowdown emerge and 
if inflation conditions permit. We forecast one more rate cut this year, bringing the federal 
funds rate to a year-end target range of 3.50%–3.75%, with additional cuts in 2026. However, 
a potential scenario exists in which the Fed may be unable to cut rates next year, particularly 
if inflation were to rise. 
We expect that U.S. Treasury yields across all maturities will be influenced by forthcoming 
Fed policy decisions. If the Fed maintains a dovish stance, two-year U.S. Treasury yields 
could decline, potentially falling below 3.5%. Meanwhile, we anticipate 10-year U.S. Treasury 
yields will remain within their current trading range of 4.00%–4.50% through year-end. 
Should a gradual economic slowdown unfold over the next few months, we would expect 
intermediate- and long-term bond yields also to trend lower. Yet, given our expectation 
for an economic recovery to gain footing in early 2026, we anticipate intermediate- and 
long-term bond yields will likely remain above 4.0%. 
Fixed-income guidance and portfolio implications

Global economic summary.
United States.
The U.S. economy maintained solid momentum through September, 
on track to register the strongest back-to-back quarterly GDP growth 
rates since early in the pandemic-related recovery. September 
business surveys from the Institute for Supply Management reflected 
moderating services-led growth masking manufacturing weakness. 
Consumer spending remained resilient through August despite more 
modest income gains. Upper-income households continue to drive 
a disproportionate share of consumer-spending growth, supported 
by the recent rally in stocks and other financial assets. Lower oil 
prices and easing rental inflation have boosted purchasing power 
and contributed to resilient spending by more financially strained 
lower-income groups. Elsewhere, investment spending remains 
powered by artificial intelligence (AI) and related spending on utilities, 
while housing-market activity perked up following a late-summer 
decline in mortgage rates.
Despite resilient economic activity, the Fed has shifted its focus to 
a softening labor market. Weakening job growth has been led by 
declines in economically sensitive employment, cushioned only by 
moderating gains in less economically sensitive sectors including 
health care, education, and government. Lingering policy uncertainties 
have stalled hiring, though businesses also appear reluctant to lay off 
workers. The September Consumer Price Index (CPI) report cemented 
another Fed interest-rate cut on October 29, showing inflation still 
low enough to allow policymakers to focus on a softening job market. 
Twelve-month CPI inflation rose to 3.0%, from 2.9% in August, amid 
firmer food, energy, and trade-sensitive core goods prices. Rental 
disinflation and a surprise decline in non-rental services costs were 
mitigating factors restraining inflation's rise.

Europe.
The eurozone economy continued to improve in September, with the 
composite purchasing managers’ index (PMI) capping a four-month 
rise to a May 2024 high. Still, concerns persist over the durability of 
the eurozone’s recovery amid lingering U.S. tariff uncertainty and tepid 
global trade. Services-led growth, especially in Germany (the heart of 
the region’s economy), sustained overall activity, while manufacturing 
activity struggled to maintain recent momentum and slipped back 
into contraction. France’s economy remains pressured by political 
turmoil and budgetary problems. Eurozone CPI inflation accelerated in 
September to a 12-month rate of 2.2% from 2.0% in August. European 
Central Bank (ECB) officials likely will respond to firmer growth and 
inflation by leaving the benchmark policy rate unchanged at their 
October policy meeting. However, prospects for renewed rate cuts may 
improve later this year if, as we expect, growth slows, and inflation 
reverses its recent rise to close below the ECB’s 2.0% target at year-end.
Asia.
Slight improvement in China’s September manufacturing and services 
activity still netted to stall-speed growth. China’s economy remains 
fragile, hampered by ongoing headwinds tied to tepid domestic demand, 
cuts in industrial overcapacity, weak private investment, a property 
slump, and insufficient government stimulus. Manufacturing activity was 
mixed elsewhere in Asia. Activity in tech-focused South Korea edged into 
expansion for the first time since January on optimism around stronger 
demand, while Vietnam and Thailand held in modest growth territory. 
However, U.S. tariff increases appear to be taking a toll on factory 
demand elsewhere in the region, with the Philippines joining Japan, 
Taiwan, and Malaysia in contraction. Extended U.S. dollar weakness 
has accommodated interest-rate cuts by several emerging-market 
central banks this year, helping temper the hit to their export-oriented 
economies from burdensome U.S. tariffs.

Wells Fargo Investment Institute forecasts
Gross domestic product (GDP) growth: U.S. growth prospects 
through 2026 have improved as the economy seeks to build on 
impressive, near-4% growth in the spring and summer. We still 
expect a mild growth slowdown in the fourth quarter of this year 
and into 2026, following what has been an unsustainable pace. We 
believe that will be followed by a moderate growth recovery during 
much of 2026, bringing the full-year pace to 2.4% from 2.0% in 2025. 
However, our anticipated soft patch at the turn of the year is being 
diluted by a more muted tariff shock, added policy stimulus, and by 
a rebound tied to the government’s reopening from the shutdown’s 
disruptive effects early in this year’s fourth quarter. 
Moreover, growth’s tailwinds this year remain intact from the stock 
market’s rally, benefiting upper-income wealth and spending, ample 
market liquidity propelling those market gains, and by Fed rate cuts, 
which have supported all three. Additional support has come from 
inflation rising more gradually than expected, lessening the pressure 
on household spending power. Looking ahead, added policy stimulus, 
early in 2026, will include tax refunds tied to July’s One Big Beautiful 
Bill Act (OBBBA), deregulation’s cost savings, and up to $1 trillion in 
refunded import duties, if the Supreme Court rules against many of 
this year’s tariff increases.
We believe that our expectation for lagging global growth through 
2026 will widen the gap with the United States. Structural 
advantages — including a dynamic tech sector, favorable 
demographics, and efficient financial markets — continue to support 
U.S. outperformance, in our view. Interest rates lifted by budget 
problems in parts of Europe may limit the impact of fiscal stimulus 
in Germany and in other countries, while monetary easing is widely 
expected to end in Europe and tighten in Japan. A firmer U.S. dollar 
could constrain rate-cutting by emerging-market central banks, raise 
the local-currency equivalent of foreign-debt costs, and dampen 
commodity prices. Additionally, the more trade-sensitive economies 
abroad are bracing for the brunt of U.S. tariff increases on exports to 
wash ashore in 2026. 
Risks to the outlook remain centered on policy uncertainties, interest 
rates, and financial-market stability. In the U.S., the timing and scale 
of further tariff increases — and their impact on consumers — could 
threaten the 2026 recovery. Higher long-term rates, driven by fiscal 
strains, political uncertainties, or fresh budget concerns, could also 
lead to tighter credit conditions in parts of Europe.
CPI inflation: We expect U.S. CPI inflation to rise moderately through 
the early part of 2026 before easing enough to leave the year-end 
rate at 2.8% from our estimate of 3.0% at the end of 2025. Early-year 
inflation will likely be driven by increased tariff passthrough, propelled 
both by greater clarity over the trade-policy outlook and by likely 
increases in tariffs over the course of next year. However, in our view, 
overall price pressures will be restrained by easing rental inflation. 
We also are counting on productivity gains, tied to stronger economic 
growth through much of 2026, to take much of the pressure off labor 
costs adjusted for the amount of output the worker produces. We 
look to these sources of disinflation as outweighing inflation’s modest 
pickup in food, energy, and, ultimately, rents later in the year.
We expect disinflation abroad to mirror the U.S. trend but from lower 
levels, leaving eurozone inflation below 2% by year-end 2026. We 
expect China to emerge from deflation — but with average inflation 
for the year likely below 1% — supported by consumer-focused 
stimulus. We believe Japan’s inflation rate will retreat below 2% as 
slower economic growth and easing food prices outweigh increased 
wage pressures. These trends should keep market-based interest

Labor market conditions: Labor-supply constraints and uncertain 
demand remain central to our 2026 labor-market outlook. We 
continue to expect the unemployment rate to rise gradually to 
4.9% in the fourth quarter of 2026, up from 4.5% in late 2025. 
This increase reflects both the unwinding of pandemic-era labor 
hoarding, the lagged effects of slower growth, and lingering 
policy uncertainties. However, immigration-related shortages are 
intensifying, particularly in sectors like agribusiness, construction, 
health care, and hospitality. The situation is exacerbated by the 
squeeze from increased retirements tied to an aging workforce. The 
Pew Research Center estimates a shortfall of 1.2 million workers 
as of July 2025, potentially rising to 2 million due to tighter border 
controls and lingering pandemic disruptions.3 These shortages 
risk pressuring wage inflation by squeezing labor supply in certain 
industries, especially in regions with high dependence on immigrant 
labor. An added wild card in the outlook for labor demand and the 
unemployment rate’s trajectory is the chance that layoffs will be 
restrained by an unexpectedly mild economic-growth slowdown

Interest rates: The Fed is a dual-mandate central bank focused on 
both price stability (inflation) and full employment. Labor-market 
data has continued to show weakness and highlights falling 
confidence in the U.S. labor market. However, the potential impact 
of tariffs on inflation remains a pain point for future Fed rate policy. 
We expect the Fed to deliver three additional interest-rate cuts 
between now and year-end 2026. Our year-end 2026 target range 
for the federal funds rate is between 3.00% and 3.25%. Our base case 
is that one cut will be delivered in the remainder of 2025, followed 
by two additional cuts in early 2026; however, there is also a 
possibility that volatile inflation and economic data may impact the 
timing of these cuts. 
We expect short-term U.S. Treasury rates to decline in tandem 
with the federal funds rate. Longer-term yields in the coming 
quarters may stay elevated near current levels under a confluence 
of crosscurrents, including variable inflation and economic growth 
as well as additional U.S. Treasury issuance and likely wider federal 
deficits. However, a more aggressive Fed easing cycle should reset 
interest-rate levels across the entire curve. If growth resumes and 
inflation expectations remain anchored, the curve will continue to 
steepen but at a lower interest-rate level than we had previously 
anticipated, as investor demand for duration increases. For year-end 
2025, our 10-year U.S. Treasury yield target stands between 4.00% 
and 4.50%, while our 30-year U.S. Treasury yield stands between 
4.50%–5.00%. For year-end 2026, the targets are the same as 
year-end 2025. This essentially keeps longer-term yields range 
bound over the next 15 months.
Equities: Monetary easing, fiscal spending, a resilient consumer, an 
AI capex cycle, and a robust economy should propel equity markets 
higher through year-end 2026. Our 2026 S&P 500 Index year-end 
price target of 7,400–7,600 and our EPS target of $300 reflect our 
expectation that earnings growth will be the main driver of stock 
returns. Please see the table to right for the other asset class targets.

We believe the U.S. central bank will continue to tread cautiously,

volatility due to policy uncertainty is set to remain elevated in the

unfavorable on U.S. Long Term and Short Term Taxable Fixed

intermediate-term bonds is preferable to over-allocating to

DM ex-U.S. Fixed Income.

local-currency denominated, should continue to display positive 
performance in the last quarter of 2025. However, most of the 
support may come on the back of additional interest-rate cuts by 
the Fed. Still, we believe the attractive yield differential of EM bonds 
can help cushion against capital losses if interest rates climb once

those seeking tax-efficient yield and diversification. We expect

to garner investor appetite, especially given the expected limited 
new issuance in the Preferred space. However, they are best suited

the Residential Mortgage-Backed Securities (RMBS) sub-sector, on

may be positioned to offer value relative to other fixed-income 
sectors while still providing favorable credit quality and liquidity.

remains visible in valuations. We remain neutral on Commercial 
Mortgage-Backed Securities (CMBS). Although there is still distress 
in CMBS, we believe it should be less severe than previously feared. 
Still, we favor staying in the highest credit qualities that may 
potentially provide more reliable cash flows. We are also favorable 
on Asset-Backed Securities (ABS). Demand for high quality ABS 
remains strong, and we still believe credit spreads have room to 
tighten further once we move past this period of uncertainty.

of U.S. Municipal Bonds and believe that the sector’s increased 
volatility during the first half of 2025 created an attractive entry

issuance to remain ample, particularly as we move further into 
the fall months. We believe demand is expected to be healthy and 
counterbalance rising supply. In late September, municipal-to-

yield curve (intermediate term) has become more attractive as the

The complexity premium potentially offered with private placements results from several 
structural limitations associated with mutual funds, including provisions of the Investment 
Company Act of 1940, as amended (1940 Act), that apply at the fund level and not the 
individual strategy level. The 1940 Act requires, among others, the following:
	F Regular liquidity — Redemptions must be paid within seven calendar days
	F Regular transparency
	F Limits on leverage — 300% asset coverage limits leverage to 33%; making loans; or 
investing in real estate or commodities
	F Limits on concentration — 75% of the value of its total assets cannot be invested more 
than 5% in any one issuer, 25% in one industry or 10% of the outstanding voting securities 
of the issuer
	F Limits on illiquidity — No more than 15% can be invested in illiquid assets
In addition, under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, performance-based fees must be 
symmetric.
As a result of the illiquidity and complexity premiums, performance returns and characteristics 
are expected to vary between liquid alternative mutual funds and private placements. 
In our view, when implementing liquid alternatives in a diversified portfolio, they should not 
be considered a one-to-one substitute for traditional hedge funds. Our new guidance will 
reflect these differences in product types.
It is important to remember that only “accredited investors” or “qualified purchasers” within 
the meaning of U.S. securities laws can invest in private placements. This means investors 
must have a minimum level of income, assets, or net worth to be eligible. They may also 
need to meet other qualification requirements. Like all mutual funds, liquid alternative funds 
are regulated under the 1940 Act, and are open to all investors. As such, they are regulated 
in their use of leverage and have required levels of liquidity and diversification. Mutual funds 
must value their portfolios and price their securities daily using fair value guidelines. 
Hedge funds, on the other hand, face less regulation and are not required to provide 
investors with periodic pricing or valuation. This allows them a great deal of flexibility but 
may increase the risks for investors.
Because of the illiquid and complex nature of private placement 
hedge funds, Wells Fargo Investment Institute will no longer provide 
tactical percentage guidance for these asset classes. We will instead 
provide guidance that may be incorporated into portfolios over a 
longer period of time.
Notes on alternative investment structures
The core differences between our guidance for private placements versus liquid alternative 
mutual funds centers on the expected illiquidity premium and the expected complexity 
premium often associated with private placements. The illiquidity premium refers to the 
potential for incremental return or yield generated by owning securities that cannot be sold 
quickly without affecting the price. Certain securities may be illiquid for one month, quarter, 
several years or longer. This illiquidity may provide investment managers enhanced flexibility 
which may result in higher long-term returns. Illiquidity may be experienced in public and 
private credit securities that can include loans, securitized credit, and stressed and distressed 
corporate credit. However, equity strategies may also be illiquid for periods of time, especially 
after a corporate restructuring when debt is converted to equity or within strategies that 
require significant equity ownership such as Activism. A complexity premium may also be 
associated with illiquid securities as they often require specialized origination, underwriting 
and investing strategies. Because private placements do not offer daily liquidity to their 
investors, they potentially provide greater flexibility to invest in securities that may offer an 
illiquidity premium. Furthermore, private placements can have a larger concentration in 
illiquid securities.

maturity curve, driven by volatility around the Fed’s mid-September 
rate cut and subsequent release of economic projections. Market 
expectations for additional Fed rate cuts in 2025 rose slightly 
as the Fed delivered on the expected rate cut; however, rate cut 
expectations for 2026 were tempered by the Fed’s projections. Fed 
policy actions — more so than those from other major central banks 
— over the next few months, coupled with potential political and 
trade risks both in the U.S. and abroad, will likely remain key factors 
for the U.S. dollar’s near-term levels. The likelihood of volatility in 
currency markets has risen, with downside potential from the dollar’s 
current levels being a key concern. DM currencies were mixed 
against the U.S. dollar in September, with the yen struggling amid
